_doc: T-3645: the 1904 'Ask a question' answers (data/tales/1904.json asks and personal_asks, shown by js/ask-card.js) retold for younger readers. Keyed by the question's id, a follow-up by that id and its place among the follow-ups (a04-md-day.1); each age a list of paragraphs, one for each of the answer's own, in the speaker's own voice. Most answers already read at 8-10 and need nothing here. Only the younger ages are written; the answer itself is never rewritten, and no fact enters that it does not hold.

8-10: At half past five, before the family wakes up. I lay the fires, even in summer, because of the damp. I scrub the front steps and polish the brass on the door. I sweep the dining room and set the breakfast table. All that is done before eight. Then I do the bedrooms after the family goes down, and the stairs, and the silver.

When the family has gone to bed and the last tray has come down. That is ten or eleven at night. Thursday afternoon and every other Sunday are mine. On Thursday all the maids from the Avenue go out at once, in our best hats. The ladies have no idea how much we know about each other's houses.

I go to the lake if it is nice. Or I look in the shops on State Street, or I see a variety show. Since the Iroquois Theatre burned last December, none of us goes near a big theatre. I go to the park and sit by the water and do nothing at all. That is the finest thing in the world.

Everyone in Chicago knows somebody who was there. It was 30 December, at an afternoon show. The theatre was packed with moms and kids for the Christmas play. The stage caught fire. The fire curtain did not come down. The doors opened inward. Six hundred people died in fifteen minutes. Most were women and children.
11-13: Everyone in Chicago knows somebody who was there. It was 30 December, at an afternoon show, and the theatre was packed with mothers and children for the Christmas play. The scenery caught fire, the fire curtain did not come down, and the doors opened inward. Six hundred people died in fifteen minutes. Most of them were women and children.

8-10: Every theatre in the city was shut while inspectors checked them. They found exit doors nailed shut. They found no water in the pipes, and fire curtains that would not stop a fire. Mr. Shortall of the Humane Society has worked to protect the city's children for years. Ask him what has been done since. He will tell you it is not enough.

The bells. There is a board in the servants' hall with a little flag or bell for each room. When the lady pulls the cord in the library, the library bell rings and its flag drops. Newer houses have tubes you can talk through, and now the telephone. But I hear the bells in my sleep.

County Mayo, in Ireland. I came by way of Queenstown and New York, six years ago. My aunt worked in a house on the North Side, and she found me my first job. Now four of us from the same church back home work on Prairie Avenue. The cook in the house across the street is my second cousin.
Every Sunday morning I go to early Mass, before the family wakes. Then I come back and serve their breakfast before they go to their own church. God gets me first.

On the North Side there is a whole town of Swedes. They have their own churches and shops. They have their own papers, and dances on Saturday. The maids on Prairie Avenue come from all over. Some are Irish, and some are from Sweden or Germany or Norway. We talk to each other in a kind of English. Nobody upstairs could follow it.
11-13: On the North Side there is a whole city of Swedes, with their own churches, shops and newspapers, and dances on Saturday. On Prairie Avenue the girls are Irish, Swedish, German and Norwegian. We talk to each other in a sort of English that nobody upstairs could follow.
14-15: On the North Side there is a whole city of Swedes, with churches, shops, Swedish newspapers and dances on Saturday. On Prairie Avenue the girls are Irish, Swedish, German and Norwegian. We talk to each other in a sort of English that nobody upstairs could follow.

8-10: The cook, Mattie Williamson. She knows the lady's book of dinners better than the lady does. The maids. The men in the stable. The girls say Mrs. Glessner writes everything in her journal. She writes who came, who said what, and what they ate. Go and ask Mattie what Mr. Thomas the musician likes for dinner.

At the top of the house, in the little rooms under the roof, two to a room. They are hot in summer and cold in winter. We go up and down the back stairs, never the front. We must never be seen on the front stairs, except to clean them before the family wakes.

A bed, a stand with a wash bowl, a chair, and a chest of drawers. A holy picture and a photo of my mom. The window looks over the alley to the carriage houses. On summer nights I can hear the horses moving in their stalls, and the trains by the lake, and nothing else.

Everybody wants to go. It opened in April. It marks a hundred years since America bought Louisiana. People say it is bigger than our own fair of 1893. There is a palace of electricity and a giant bird cage. Mr. Ferris's own wheel from our fair is there, carried down and set up again. There are villages of people from all over the world that you can walk through.
11-13: Everybody wants to go. It opened in April, a hundred years after the Louisiana Purchase, and they say it is bigger than our own fair of 1893. There is a palace of electricity and a giant bird cage. Mr. Ferris's own wheel from our fair was carried down and set up again. There are villages of people from the whole world that you can walk through.

8-10: Some of the families on the Avenue went down in May in their own train cars. The servants who went came back with picture postcards. They told stories about ice cream served in a rolled waffle, which you eat, cone and all! Mr. Kimball won prizes for his pianos at our own fair in 1893. Ask him if he has sent any to St. Louis.

A whole morning every week, for two of us. We use polish and soft cloths, in a little room by the dining room, with the door shut. We do the forks, spoons, trays, candlesticks, the tea set, and the big dish for the middle of the table. Every piece is counted out and counted back.

The young ladies, calling each other about dances. Their mom says it is not ladylike to talk on the telephone. They do it anyway, in the back hall, in whispers. If their mom asks, I am supposed to say they are out.

A chicken pie. The master asks for it every Sunday. He is not supposed to have it, because the doctor says he is too fat. On Sunday I make it anyway. The lady of the house pretends not to notice. Upstairs is full of things everyone pretends not to notice.

The ice box. It is a wooden chest lined with metal. A block of lake ice goes in the top. The ice man brings it every morning, a hundred pounds on his back, held with tongs. The cold falls down onto the butter, milk and meat. The water drips into a pan. The kitchen girl empties it, if she remembers.

From the lakes and ponds north of the city. In winter men cut it into big blocks. They store it in ice houses, packed in sawdust. In July the ice man is the most popular man on the Avenue. The kids follow his wagon for the chips.

The grocer and the butcher come to the back door every morning to take the order. They bring it by noon. Once a week I go to the South Water Street market myself, early, for fish, fruit and the best vegetables. The driver takes me. It is a mile of wagons, shouting, boxes and horses.

Half the Avenue, and some men from the orchestra. Mr. Thomas, the conductor, was one. Afterward he came down to the kitchen to thank me himself. No guest had ever done that. In my heart I have been his servant ever since.

Six, in the stable behind the house. There are two pairs of carriage horses. They are brown and match perfectly. There is a small horse for the light cart, and the master's riding horse, which he does not ride as much as he should. I feed them at five. I brush them by seven. I hitch them up by nine for the master's drive to his office.

A closed carriage for the master in town. An open carriage for the lady on nice afternoons in the park. And a big closed coach for the opera and the theatre. Each one has its own harness and its own lamps. Every bit of brass must shine like a mirror. A dirty carriage is the driver's shame.

We are like a club. Every carriage house along the alley has a driver. In the evening we stand in the alley, smoking. We talk about horses and masters. We know whose horse is lame, whose stable boy drinks, and whose master is going broke, before his banker does.

Along the lake on the wide roads. Out to Washington Park and Jackson Park, where the fair was. On a summer day every carriage on the Avenue is out there. The ladies wear their summer dresses. The drivers wear their summer coats. They all go slow, so everyone can see everyone else.
11-13: Along the lake on the wide boulevards. Out to Washington Park and Jackson Park, where the fair was. On a summer day every carriage on the Avenue is out there. The ladies wear their summer dresses, and the drivers wear their summer coats. Everyone goes at a walk, so everybody can see everybody else.
14-15: Along the lake on the boulevards, out to Washington Park and Jackson Park, where the Fair was. On a summer afternoon every carriage on the Avenue is out there. The ladies are in their summer gowns and the coachmen in their summer livery. They all go at a walk, so everybody can see everybody else.

8-10: Waiting. In January I wait outside the opera, a dinner or a dance. I sit on the driver's seat with a fur robe and a lantern until two in the morning. The horses stand with their blankets on and their breath smoking, and I stand with them. You get to know a horse well on those nights.

Driving two good horses fast along the lake shore on a crisp morning. The sun comes up out of the water. Nobody is in the carriage at all, because I am just giving the horses a run. Then the horses and I are the kings of the Avenue.
11-13: Driving a pair of good horses fast on the lake shore on a crisp morning, with the sun coming up out of the water. Nobody is in the carriage at all, because I am exercising them. Then the horses and I are the masters of the Avenue.

8-10: On my dad's farm in Kerry, in Ireland. Then as a stable boy for an English family in Dublin. Then in the stables of New York, and then here. That is twenty years of horses. I can tell a horse's age by its teeth, and its mood by its ears. I can spot a bad stable boy by the horse's coat.

Calm nerves, most of all. A carriage horse in Chicago must stand still for cable cars, trains, fire engines, bands and motor cars. He must walk with a thousand other horses and not kick any of them. A horse like that is worth more than a racehorse.

Monday, every Monday. We wash in the basement. There are three big tubs, a boiler on the stove, a wringer, and a drying room with racks for rainy days. We wash all the house's cloth: every sheet, napkin, collar and slip. Tuesday is for ironing. Wednesday is for mending.

From six in the morning to six at night, for two of us. The white things are boiled. The colored things go in warm water, and the wool in cool. The master's collars are starched so stiff they could cut a finger. By evening the steam has taken the curl out of my hair and the skin off my knuckles.

Two little ones, a boy of four and a girl of two, in the nursery on the third floor. I wake them, wash them and dress them. I give them breakfast and walk them in the park. I give them lunch and put them down for their nap. At five I bring them down in their best clothes to see their mom for half an hour.
11-13: Two little ones, a boy of four and a girl of two, in the nursery on the third floor. I wake them, wash them, dress them and give them breakfast. I walk them in the park, give them their dinner and put them down for their nap. At five I bring them down to the drawing room in their best clothes, to see their mother for half an hour.

8-10: To the lake shore, or down the Avenue to the statue at Eighteenth Street. It is the bronze of the Indian chief saving the lady. The boy asks about it every time. I tell him what the policeman on the corner told me. It was a battle long ago, when Chicago was a fort, and the chief was a good man.
11-13: To the lake shore, or down the Avenue to the statue at Eighteenth Street, the bronze of the Indian chief saving the lady. The boy asks about it every time. I tell him what the policeman on the corner told me: it was a battle long ago, when Chicago was a fort, and the chief was a good man.

8-10: Everything that keeps the house running, and nothing that anyone sees. I keep the keys to the sheets, the dishes, the food and the wine. I hire and train the maids. I order the coal, soap and candles. I keep the money books. I make sure every room is ready before anyone wants it.

He answers the door and takes the visiting cards. He announces the guests. He serves the wine and carves the meat. He keeps the silver, winds the clocks and hires the footmen. He makes sure every man in the house does his work. A good butler is like a good clock. Nobody notices him until he stops.
11-13: Answer the door, take the visiting cards, announce the guests, serve the wine, carve the meat, keep the silver, wind the clocks, hire the footmen, and see that every man in the house does his work. A good butler is like a good clock. Nobody notices him until he stops.

8-10: I have announced a Vice President, three senators, two English lords, and the head of the University. And Mr. Pullman, before he died. He walked in as if he owned this house too. The great ones are easier than the rich ones. The great ones say thank you.

I am the house man. In winter I shovel coal into the furnace and carry the ashes out. I wash the windows and beat the carpets. I carry the trunks and fix what breaks. I do the heavy work the maids cannot. In summer I wash down the house and paint the iron fence.

The Board of Trade, mostly. I trade grain. That means I buy wheat that has not grown yet, from men who do not own it. Then I sell it to men who do not want it. And somehow everybody eats! My dad did it before me. It is the most important job in the world, or the silliest, depending on the day.

Glessner, at the corner of Eighteenth, for his good sense. Field, for his money. Kimball, for his music. Glessner has made farm machines since the war. Two years ago all the farm machine companies joined into one, International Harvester. He helps run it. Go and ask him about it. He thinks it is a great thing, and a sad one.

I eat lunch every day at the Chicago Club, on Michigan Avenue. I argue about politics at the Union League. I argue about the city at the Commercial Club. A man like me uses clubs the way a ship uses ports. He stops in, picks up news, and goes out again.
11-13: The Chicago Club, on Michigan Avenue, where I eat lunch every day. The Union League, where I argue about politics. The Commercial Club, where I argue about the city. A man in my place belongs to clubs the way a ship belongs to harbors: he stops in, picks up the news, and goes out again.
14-15: The Chicago Club, on Michigan Avenue, where I have lunch every day. The Union League, where I argue about politics. And the Commercial Club, where I argue about the city. A man in my position belongs to clubs as a ship belongs to harbors: he calls in, picks up the news, and goes out again.

8-10: The big party meeting and Mr. Roosevelt. The war in the Far East between Japan and Russia. Japan is winning, and nobody thought it would. Mr. Burnham's plan for the lake front. And the price of beef. Always the price of beef.
11-13: The convention and Mr. Roosevelt. The war in the Far East between the Japanese and the Russians, which the Japanese are winning against all odds. Mr. Burnham's plan for the lake front. And the price of beef, always the price of beef.

8-10: I was twenty in 1871. I stood on the lake shore with my mom and my sisters. We had our silver in a pillowcase. We watched the city burn behind us for two days. It was so hot that people waded into the lake. In the morning there was nothing left between the river and Fullerton but chimneys.

A few of the young men have. They race them on the wide streets at dawn, and the police chase them on bikes. George Glessner, up the Avenue, has read everything about them. Ask him if he thinks they will last.

The University of Chicago stands next to them, on the Midway. It is made of gray stone, in the English style. It is a dozen years old and grows every year. Mr. Rockefeller gave the money, and Mr. Field gave the land. The Field Museum is in the old art building in Jackson Park. It is full of everything the fair left behind.
11-13: The University of Chicago stands beside them, on the Midway. It is built of gray stone in the English style. It is a dozen years old and grows every year. Mr. Rockefeller gave the money and Mr. Field gave the land. The Field Museum is in the fair's old Fine Arts building in Jackson Park, full of everything the fair left behind.

8-10: I help the nurses who visit sick people at home. I help a home for people with no family. I sew for the Children's Hospital. Every winter I help raise money for coal. The poor of this city freeze in winter and boil in summer. A lady with time and money must do what she can.
11-13: The Visiting Nurse Association, the Home for the Friendless, a sewing group for the Children's Hospital, and every winter a committee to buy coal for the poor. The poor of this city freeze in winter and boil in summer. A lady with time and money must do what she can.
14-15: The Visiting Nurse Association, the Home for the Friendless, a sewing circle for the Children's Hospital, and every winter a committee to raise money for coal. The poor of this city freeze in winter and boil in summer. A lady with time and money must do what she can.

8-10: Twice. Miss Addams herself showed us around. There is a nursery, a kindergarten, classes for working girls, a gym and a coffee house. It is all in the middle of the poorest part of the West Side. It made me ashamed of my fancy living room. Mrs. Armour gives to the poor more quietly than anyone on the Avenue. Ask her about her husband's school.

Two of them. One meets on Michigan Avenue to hear talks about books and history. The other does good works and argues about voting. We can vote for the school board and the heads of the state college, and that is all. We are told to be happy with that.
11-13: The Fortnightly, which meets in its rooms on Michigan Avenue to hear talks on books and history. And the Woman's Club, which does good works and argues about the vote. We can vote for the school board and the University of Illinois trustees, and nothing else. We are told to be content.

8-10: Every Friday afternoon in the season. We sit in our own box at the Auditorium. Mr. Thomas plays Beethoven and Wagner and new music too. The ladies of Chicago sit and listen in their hats. Some of us get it. All of us like to be seen.

Mr. Thomas has wanted his own hall for years. He wants one smaller than the Auditorium, built just for music. The people who back the orchestra raised the money last winter. It is going up now on Michigan Avenue, across from the Art Institute. They say it will open by Christmas. The Glessners were among the first to give. Ask her about it, and watch her change the subject.

Away, as soon as we can. In July the city is all dust, heat and train smoke. Some families go to Lake Geneva, some to the north shore, and some to Maine or New Hampshire. We go to our cottage at Lake Forest at the end of the week. The servants close up the house with sheets over everything.

Mostly the men. They come out on the train for the weekend. A few servants stay to keep the house, and the driver stays with the horses. The Avenue gets very quiet. In the evening the maids sit on the front steps when nobody is looking. They think nobody knows.

The best ones come from Paris, from the famous dressmakers there. We order them on our trip to Europe every other spring. The rest come from the dress shop at Field's store. It is as good as anything in New York, and costs almost as much. A lady needs a dress for the morning, one for walking, one for the afternoon, one for dinner, and one for dances. She needs a new set for each season.
11-13: The best come from Paris, from Worth or Doucet, ordered on our trip abroad every second spring. The rest come from the dressmaking rooms at Field's, which are as good as anything in New York and cost almost as much. A lady needs a morning dress, a walking dress, an afternoon dress, a dinner dress and a ball gown, and a new set for each season.

8-10: The sleeves are smaller than ten years ago, thank goodness. The skirts are longer, and the shape is curvier, which means the corsets are tighter. The young girls play golf and tennis in blouses and short skirts. Their moms are shocked. Their moms did the same with bikes.

Eleven. A butler, two footmen, a cook and a kitchen maid, two housemaids, a parlor maid, a laundress, a nurse, and the driver, with a stable boy. It sounds like a lot until you see how big the house is. A house like this is a small town, and the servants are its government.

The Cubs, of course, at the West Side Grounds. Frank Chance plays first base, Tinker plays shortstop, and Evers plays second. Everybody says they will win the pennant one of these years, if the Giants ever lose. My dad likes the White Sox, on the South Side. They are closer, and Comiskey once sold him a horse.

Everyone did ten years ago, when the new safe bikes came in. On Sunday mornings Michigan Avenue was a river of wheels. Now it is golf, tennis and motor cars. But I still ride to the lake in the mornings, before it gets hot. On a bike, nobody can tell if you are rich or poor.

The bike craze is over. The girls who fought to ride in baggy pants are married now. Their daughters play tennis in skirts. It always goes like that. The moms fight, and the daughters take it for granted.

Last winter, at a dance my mom gave at the house. The ballroom on the third floor was opened up, and the orchestra played in the hall. I wore white, of course, with my grandma's pearls. I danced every dance. I broke the heel off my slipper and had to finish in my stockings. Nobody noticed. Everybody noticed.

I do. My mom does not, and my grandma is furious about it. In Illinois we can vote for school leaders and nothing else. In Wyoming, Colorado and Utah, women vote for everything, and the sky has not fallen. My dad says politics would make women rough. I have heard my dad talk politics. I think it would make women bored.

Three more days! We'll have firecrackers, Roman candles and sparklers. There's a parade on Michigan Avenue, and lemonade. At night my dad takes us to the lake to see the rockets. Last year my brother lit a firecracker in the barn. The horses kicked their stalls. He wasn't allowed out for a week.

It shows an Indian chief stopping another Indian from hurting a lady. There is a man lying down and a little child. Mr. Pullman put it there, by his house, because that is where the fight was long ago, when Chicago was a fort. My nurse says the chief's name was Black Partridge, and he was brave.

I go to a school for boys on Michigan Avenue. The teacher has a mustache and a ruler. We learn Latin, math, geography and handwriting. I am bad at handwriting. My letters lean over as if they were tired. In the fall my sister goes to a school for girls, where they learn French and piano.

The ladies of the reading group at the Glessners' come on Mondays, all at once. So the whole street knows where they are going. In summer nobody comes at all. They are all away. The visiting cards just sit and gather dust.

A policeman. He is Irish, and he walks his beat on Michigan Avenue. At nine fifteen every night, he walks past our back steps and does not look up. At nine fifteen every night, I am at the window and do not look out. We have been sweethearts like this since Easter.

My dad found me a summer job at the big store that sells to other stores. I will count the goods and learn the business from the bottom, like he says he did. They tell me Mr. Field started as a clerk who slept under the counter. Every young man on the Avenue has heard that story a hundred times.
11-13: My father has found me a summer job in the wholesale house. I will count stock and learn the business from the bottom, as he says he did. They tell me Mr. Field started as a clerk who slept under the counter. Every young man on the Avenue has heard that story a hundred times.
14-15: My father has found me a place for the summer in the wholesale house, counting stock and learning the business from the bottom, as he says he did. Mr. Field started as a clerk sleeping under the counter, they tell me. Every young man on the Avenue has heard that story a hundred times.

8-10: It's my dad's, but I drive it, because he's afraid of it. It goes twenty miles an hour on the wide street if the police aren't looking. It breaks down every other time I take it out. I carry a toolbox, a spare tire, a can of gas, and lots of patience.

St. Luke's and the children's hospital. I go every week in the season, with the group. I read to the kids, bring oranges, and talk to the moms. It is the most useful two hours of my week, and the hardest. Some of those kids got out of the Iroquois fire with burns that will never heal.

My oldest girl is twenty. She has started going to dances and parties, and she wants to go to Europe to study music. My boy is at school in the East. He writes once a month, to ask for money. The little one is still in the nursery. She is the darling of the house, and her nurse is the boss of her.

Strict about manners, easy about everything else. My own mom was strict about everything. So I learned to do what I liked when she wasn't looking. My daughters do what they like while I am looking. I think that is better.

A uniform. It has a dark coat with brass buttons, a striped vest, black pants and white gloves. For dinners I wear short pants to the knee and silk stockings. I hate them. The family's crest is on the buttons. I am a walking ad for the house.

I like the dinners, when the house is lit and the silver shines and the talk is good. I don't like to stand behind a chair for three hours while a man talks about money. But a good footman can hear a lot while he looks at nothing.

A lady on the Avenue died last winter. The horses wore black feathers, and the hearse went first. We went at a walk all the way to the cemetery in the snow. Every carriage on the Avenue came behind us. The horses knew. They walked with their heads down, like sad people, and never took a wrong step.

The master likes plain food, and the lady likes French food. So I cook French and call it plain. The young ladies want everything from the magazines. The little ones want bread and butter. Most days I please all of them. That is more than the President can do.

Yes. I have written in it every week since 1879, here and in our old house. I write who came to dinner and what we ate. I write what was said and what the kids did. I write about the concerts, the weather, and the servants coming and going. The books are thick, with leather covers. They sit on the shelf in my room. Mr. Glessner says I am writing the story of Prairie Avenue, whether it wants one or not.

That it was very warm. That Mattie made a lemon ice. That Fanny brought the kids to lunch, and the little ones ate it all but the vegetables. That is the story of Prairie Avenue today. The rest is in the papers.

I have sewn all my life, fancy stitching and lace, the old ways. And lately I have been making things out of silver. I take lessons, with a bench and tools upstairs. My friends are amazed that a lady would hammer metal. I am amazed at how much I like it.
11-13: Needlework all my life, embroidery and lace in the old ways. And lately, silver. I have started lessons in making silver things, with a bench and tools upstairs. My friends are amazed that a lady should hammer metal. I am amazed at how much I enjoy it.

8-10: The street is the noisiest, dirtiest thing about Chicago, and the sun is the best thing. Mr. Richardson put the rooms we live in along the yard, on the south side, so light comes in all day. He put the servants' rooms along the north wall, to block the wind. The kitchen looks onto the yard too. Our cook has a better view than most of my neighbors.
The library, at the end of the evening. The fire is lit, my wife is reading, and the house is quiet. A man can run a big company all day and come home to that. Then he knows what all the work is for.

Two years ago the five big makers of farm machines joined into one company. McCormick, Deering, our own company, and two others joined. Before that, we kept cutting our prices to beat each other, and it was ruining us all. Now we build the best machines together. Mr. Morgan's bank set it up. I am one of its leaders.
11-13: Two years ago the five big harvester makers joined into one company: McCormick, Deering, our own Warder, Bushnell and Glessner, and two others. That way we stopped ruining each other by cutting prices, and built the best machines together. Mr. Morgan's bank set it up. I am a vice president and on the board.

8-10: It was the smart thing. Whether it is right, the government will decide. Some men in Washington call companies like this trusts, and they want to break them up. My old company's name is gone. My son George watched all the talks from the side of the room. Ask him what he thought of the McCormicks.

A good, plain soup, and a roast, and something with cream. He does not like anything fancy. He likes his coffee very strong, and his cigar after it in the library with Mr. Glessner. When he is coming, the lady tells me the day before, and I make his favorites. He always has seconds. He says it is Beethoven in a pudding.
11-13: A good plain soup, and a roast, and something with cream. He does not care for anything fussy. He likes his coffee very strong and his cigar after it in the library with Mr. Glessner. When he comes, the mistress tells me the day before, and I make his favorites. He always eats a second helping and says it is Beethoven in a pudding.

8-10: The kitchen is on the north side, along Eighteenth Street. Its windows look onto the yard, so I get the light and not the dust. There is a big stove, a washing room beside it, the pantries, and the servants' hall where we eat. Christine and Mary come through all day for the trays. I was born in Quebec to Irish parents. I can feed a Frenchman, an Irishman and a Yankee and please all three. I hear every step on the back stairs, and I know whose it is.

It is a school on Thirty-third Street. It is for young men and women from working families. They learn to build bridges, houses and engines. They learn about chemicals and electricity. These are the skills that will build this country. My husband built the school with a minister, Dr. Gunsaulus. He gave it millions. Since he died, I have kept it going.
11-13: It is a school on Thirty-third Street for young men and women from working families. They learn engineering, how to design buildings, chemistry and electricity. These are the trades that will build this country. My husband built it with Dr. Gunsaulus, the minister, and gave it millions. Since he died, I have carried on what he began.

8-10: Every morning I can. I walk up Prairie and Michigan to State and Washington. That is about three miles. A man who sits in a carriage misses the city. On foot I see the shop windows and the crowds. I see what people wear and carry, and which streets are busy. By the time I get to my desk, I know more about business than my managers.

Quietly. I do not like seeing my name in the newspapers for giving money away. Mrs. Armour, down the Avenue, gives even more quietly. She has built something better than most men have with twice the money. Go and ask her about the school.

I answer the door and show in the visitors. I serve at the table and bring the tea in the afternoon. I keep the parlor and the library neat. I dust the books, arrange the flowers and polish the tables. I never move anything Mrs. Glessner has put in its place. I see everyone who comes into this house, and they all see me. None of them remembers my face.
11-13: I answer the door, show in the visitors, serve at table, and bring the tea in the afternoon. I keep the parlor and the library in order. I dust the books, arrange the flowers and polish the tables, and I never move anything Mrs. Glessner has placed. I see everyone who comes into this house, and they all see me. None of them remembers my face.
14-15: I answer the door, show in the callers, wait at table, and bring the tea in the afternoon. I keep the parlor and the library in order: I dust the books, arrange the flowers, polish the tables, and never move anything Mrs. Glessner has placed. I see everyone who comes into this house, and they all see me, and none of them remembers my face.

8-10: We have shared the back stairs since the family moved in. We know each other's steps and each other's moods. She has the parlor and the visitors. I have the bedrooms and the sheets. In the great fire, every record in the city burned. After that, the only proof of who owns what was in private books like ours. So the state made our books count as proof in court. Every piece of land in Chicago depends on them. Under it all, a city is only paper. Who owns this land? Who owes that money?
